content: First, we need to clearly define what constitutes excellent design. Excellent design must first comply with all applicable codes, standards, and regulatory requirements—this is the most fundamental prerequisite. Secondly, since design documents will guide the construction and tendering processes, they must clearly and accurately define the scope of work.

Excellent design also requires comprehensive consideration of the following key factors:  
1. Upon project completion, it must provide clients or end-users with outstanding technical performance metrics while delivering cost-effective technical solutions.  
2. Constructability must be thoroughly considered during the design phase to ensure the feasibility of the proposed solutions.  
3. For MEP (mechanical, electrical, and plumbing) disciplines, designed systems must facilitate ease of future maintenance and operation.  

Currently, energy efficiency and environmental sustainability have become global priorities, with many regions including North America and China placing significant emphasis on them. In cities across Vancouver and British Columbia, energy performance metrics have become critical approval criteria, even directly influencing building permit issuance. Furthermore, excellent design should optimize project scheduling to achieve shortened construction timelines.

Next, we will explore the concept of Peer Review. Peer Review is an evaluation process conducted by a third party rather than the original designer. This third party can be non-design personnel from the same design firm or professionals from external peer design companies.

In North America, the design phase is typically divided into: Schematic Design, 66% Design Phase, 99% Building Permit Design Phase, as well as the Issue for Tender (IFT) Phase and the Issue for Construction Phase. Peer Review is primarily conducted during the 66% and 99% design phases.

Due to the additional costs involved, owners of small projects are often reluctant to conduct Peer Review. However, for medium to large projects, especially those with high specialization or significance, owners frequently require Peer Review. Such reviews are usually performed by senior designers with extensive experience and expertise in specific fields.

Although Peer Review is not mandatory, it holds significant value: First, it can identify potential issues in the design, thereby mitigating design and construction risks. Second, Peer Review helps owners optimize design solutions, potentially achieving cost savings or schedule reductions, for example, by proposing superior design alternatives.

Value Engineering primarily includes the following aspects:

First is design optimization, a process that occurs before construction begins. Value Engineering is a systematic approach that, compared to construction and project costs, is relatively low-cost yet can significantly reduce expenses. Its objective is to provide the necessary reliable functions at the lowest possible cost. This method employs structured and systematic problem-solving strategies and strives to explore constructive and creative alternatives.

Below we outline the objectives of Value Engineering.

Below we outline the objectives of Value Engineering.

First, Value Engineering can save time costs and energy. Second, it helps project teams make decisions quickly. In large-scale projects, multiple departments are typically involved, such as design, project management, construction, commissioning, the client, and construction supervision. These different stakeholders need to coordinate collectively when making project decisions. Value Engineering provides an excellent platform to bring all relevant parties together for consultation, ultimately leading to optimized decisions.

Another objective of Value Engineering is to identify and mitigate risks in engineering projects at an early stage. Through Value Engineering, resource and time wastage in projects can be minimized. Cost savings essentially translate to value addition for the project. For example, if the original plan was to invest 1 million yuan to complete the project and sell it for 2 million yuan, but the project was actually completed for only 800,000 yuan while still selling for 2 million yuan, then the project achieves an added value of 200,000 yuan.

The advantages of value engineering lie in its ability to simplify complex project implementation methods and processes, enhance efficiency, and avoid recurring costs. Additionally, value engineering facilitates project communication, enabling all parties to gain a more accurate and efficient understanding of the project. It provides an opportunity for owners and various departments involved in project design and construction to engage in collaborative discussions, particularly during the design phase, thereby improving communication efficiency among stakeholders.
During the peer review and value engineering process, we typically need to examine the following aspects:

Check for over-specification. Over-specification refers to the use of unnecessary, high-cost design methods to achieve certain objectives, where such excessive requirements are not mandated by the project itself or regulatory standards, leading to wasteful spending for the owner. Such issues are typically identified during peer reviews and value engineering analyses.

Article 7 also requires checking whether the MEP (Mechanical, Electrical, Plumbing) design involves oversized equipment or system capacity selection. Oversizing similarly results in financial waste for the owner. Therefore, systems and equipment should be selected to match actual needs, ensuring compliance with design requirements and standards while saving costs for the client.

Next, evaluate whether there are opportunities to use materials and equipment with higher cost-performance ratios during the design process.

Next, evaluate whether there are opportunities to use materials and equipment with higher cost-performance ratios during the design process.

The following article calls for assessing whether alternative solutions exist beyond the current design that could reduce project costs.

Furthermore, for MEP disciplines (e.g., water, gas, electricity), multiple options are often available. For instance, in electrical design, the project team must evaluate whether to use 600V, 208V, or 15,000V high-voltage power supply, as different design approaches impact project costs differently.

Lastly, explore feasible solutions to further optimize project expenditures.

We can consider importing some materials and equipment from China to reduce material and equipment costs. However, it is important to note that all equipment and materials imported for use in Canadian projects must be CSA certified, which is a mandatory requirement. Many clients have incurred significant waste due to unawareness of this. It is advisable to complete the certification in the exporting country to avoid potential high costs, long cycles, and risks of non-compliance when certifying in Canada.

Additionally, construction methods should be a focus during value engineering reviews. For example, modular design is widely adopted in oilfield projects, such as pipelines, cable trays, and platforms. Modular design can significantly reduce costs, as factory manufacturing is far cheaper than on-site assembly. This advantage is particularly evident in Alberta’s oil industry, as well as in commercial construction. Modularization not only saves expenses but can also substantially shorten project timelines.

Lastly, during value engineering and peer reviews, it is also necessary to evaluate whether the design can accelerate project progress. Time cost is critical—if a project extends from six months to ten months, the additional four months will incur substantial extra expenses. For projects urgently needing to commence production, a four-month delay represents significant waste and may even result in penalties. Therefore, project schedule management is equally vital.

Next, we will explain how to prepare a Value Engineering Document.

Typically, personnel conducting peer reviews will prepare a log file, as shown here. This file includes design documents such as overviews, technical specifications, and drawings. The drawings section will be accompanied by review comments.

Subsequently, the log file will be sent to the design consultant or client, who will review the comments and provide responses or decisions on whether to adopt the proposed modifications.

The above is an explanation regarding the log file.

In addition, there are meeting minutes for the review sessions. These minutes are compiled by the session chair and distributed to all attendees. After the peer review and value engineering meetings, the design consultant and the owner will jointly discuss and decide which recommendations should be implemented, which should be temporarily shelved, and which should be rejected. This is the follow-up work required by the owner and the design team after the meetings.

Typically, the design professionals involved in peer reviews do not assume any responsibility or risk, but they provide reasonable suggestions based on their expertise and experience. Engineering and architectural associations in Canadian provinces have developed guidelines for peer reviews, clarifying the specific review process and defining the roles and responsibilities between design engineers/architects and reviewing engineers/architects. These documents provide detailed guidance on the division of duties among all parties.

Below I will briefly introduce several project cases I have participated in, including peer review, value engineering, and a negative example of construction losses caused by poor design, to emphasize the importance of prioritizing design.

Guelph University Laboratory Design Review: The firm specialized in biochemical laboratory design and undertook multiple peer review projects—this was one of them.

Montreal Hospital Design Review: Another biochemical laboratory-related review. I was primarily responsible for the electrical discipline review, leveraging extensive experience in biochemical lab design.

Finally, I’ll share a case of significant losses due to neglecting design: a pulp mill project in BC. When I took over as head of the electrical and control department, the design was already completed. The project was led by an Asian company that, in pursuit of efficiency, rushed to tender when only 60% of the design was finalized, planning to resolve issues during construction. This approach ultimately led to substantial cost overruns—a profound lesson.

When I joined the project, the design work had already been completed, and construction had commenced. However, during the construction process, I discovered numerous design flaws, inadequacies, and even errors. These defects all had to be rectified during the construction phase, causing the cost of the electrical and instrumentation portion to skyrocket from the originally planned 5-6 million yuan to 12 million yuan—a doubling of the budget. The project timeline also extended from the anticipated 3-6 months to nearly a year.

This case illustrates that design is the foundation of a project. If there are deficiencies in the design phase, they will lead to numerous issues during construction and project operation: technical challenges that cannot be resolved, increased costs due to design oversights, and project delays caused by design changes. Severe design mistakes may even result in project failure.

It is worth noting that design fees typically account for only 5%-10% of the total project cost, and for residential projects, this can go up to 12%. If the client cuts costs excessively in this phase, engineers and architects will lack sufficient resources to optimize the design, only meeting basic regulatory requirements. Conversely, appropriately increasing investment in design can lead to greater cost savings through optimized solutions.

The above serves as a brief introduction to Peer Review and Value Engineering, and I hope it provides valuable insights for everyone.
